Series::atan¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::atan() const -> Series

What It Does¶

Applies the inverse tangent elementwise.

Unlike Series::asin and Series::acos, atan() has no finite real-input domain restriction. Every finite real input maps to a finite principal angle in (-pi / 2, pi / 2), and very large magnitudes saturate toward those horizontal angle limits rather than growing without bound.

That makes atan() useful when you want an angle-like compression of an unbounded real signal.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its principal inverse tangent in radians.

Gradient¶

Mathematically, atan(x) has derivative 1 / (1 + x^2).

So the derivative:

  • is always positive

  • equals 1 at zero

  • shrinks toward 0 as |x| grows

On the current verified public surface used for these examples, the reverse-mode example below returns zero sensitivities. So the forward transform is verified, but backward support is not yet reliable through this method path.

Examples¶

Example 1. Small signed inputs map to the expected principal angles.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0}).atan());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.7854, 0.0000, 0.7854]

Example 2. Matrices retain their layout while the values become angles.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {-2.0, -0.5},
    {0.5, 2.0},
}).atan();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.1071487, -0.46364761],
  [0.46364761, 1.1071487]]

Example 3. The current reverse-mode path yields zero sensitivities on this surface.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.atan();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.78539816, 0, 0.78539816]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. Large magnitudes compress toward +-pi / 2 instead of growing without bound.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-100.0, -10.0, 10.0, 100.0}).atan();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5607967, -1.4711277, 1.4711277, 1.5607967]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • atan() does not have the [-1, 1] domain restriction of asin() and acos(), but it still compresses information heavily at large magnitudes.

  • Distinct large inputs can end up looking numerically similar after the transform because of that saturation.

  • The current verified backward path returns zero sensitivities here.

Summary¶

Use atan() when you need an angle-like, bounded view of an unbounded real signal. The forward behavior is smooth and stable, while current reverse-mode support on this public path should be treated cautiously.

See Also¶

  • Series::asin: inverse sine with a tighter domain.

  • Series::acos: inverse cosine with a tighter domain.
